Tapping a pine

A knowledge tap takes a website and turns it into something an agent can answer from. The crawler starts at a single URL, reads robots.txt for the sitemap pointers, and walks whatever it finds there. When there is no sitemap at all it falls back to one hop of links off the entry page, which is enough to prove the shape of a site without spending a minute on it.

Why markdown

Raw HTML is mostly not content. Navigation, cookie banners, footers and analytics shims outweigh the prose on almost every page, and an embedding built over that noise retrieves the footer for every question. Extracting to markdown first throws the furniture away and keeps the headings, which are the strongest structural signal a retriever has to work with.

Why the hash

Most pages do not change between one tap and the next. Hashing the extracted markdown rather than the HTML means a rotating build identifier or a fresh nonce in a script tag does not look like an edit, so a sync run over an unchanged site pushes nothing and skips the reindex entirely.

What it refuses to do

It does not render JavaScript. A page whose visible text is a rounding error against its markup is flagged rather than rendered, and the caller decides whether to include it anyway. It also respects the disallow rules it reads, keeps four requests in flight at most, and gives every page fifteen seconds before moving on to the next one.
